umbrellas.title: THE SIX UMBRELLAS
umbrellas.intro: Every enduring issue fits under one of these six. Spot the umbrella fast. Then name the exact issue underneath it, and explain it.

items.name: POWER & ITS ABUSE
items.question: Who holds authority, and what happens to the people who did not choose them.
items.issues: Abuse of Power · Imperialism · Human Rights Violations · Inequality

issue_defs.name: Abuse of Power
issue_defs.definition: when someone with authority uses it to harm people or to serve themselves.

issue_defs.name: Imperialism
issue_defs.definition: when a stronger country takes control of another land and its people.

issue_defs.name: Human Rights Violations
issue_defs.definition: when people are denied the basic rights every person should have, like life, freedom and safety.

issue_defs.name: Inequality
issue_defs.definition: when some groups get fewer rights, chances or resources than others.

items.name: CONFLICT
items.question: Why people fight, and what is still unsettled when the fighting stops.

issue_defs.name: Conflict
issue_defs.definition: a struggle between groups, nations or ideas, from argument to war.

items.name: IDENTITY & NATIONALISM
items.question: Who a people say they are, and who that leaves out.

issue_defs.name: Nationalism
issue_defs.definition: a people's loyalty to their own nation, and the push for that nation to rule itself.

issue_defs.name: Cultural Exchange and Diffusion
issue_defs.definition: when ideas, beliefs, goods and ways of life spread from one people to another.

items.name: WEALTH & RESOURCES
items.question: Who owns what a place produces, and who does the producing.

issue_defs.name: Economic Development
issue_defs.definition: how a place grows its wealth, and who that growth helps or leaves behind.

issue_defs.name: Scarcity
issue_defs.definition: not having enough of something people need, like food, water or land.

items.name: TECHNOLOGY & ENVIRONMENT
items.question: What new tools let people do, and what they cost the world around them.
items.issues: Scientific and Technological Change · Environmental Crisis

issue_defs.name: Scientific and Technological Change
issue_defs.definition: new knowledge and tools that change how people live and work.

issue_defs.name: Environmental Crisis
issue_defs.definition: serious harm to land, air, water or climate, often caused by people.

items.name: A CONNECTED WORLD
items.question: What happens when distant places start depending on each other.

issue_defs.name: Cooperation
issue_defs.definition: when groups or countries work together toward a shared goal.

issue_defs.name: Population and Migration
issue_defs.definition: how the number of people in a place changes, and why people move.

close: On the essay, write the exact issue, not the umbrella: “Human Rights Violations,” not “Power & Its Abuse.”
Then EXPLAIN IT: define the problem in one sentence, and show where a document shows it.

casefiles.title: 10.3 Casefile A · Why did the Industrial Revolution begin in Great Britain?

docs.title: The Agricultural Revolution in Britain
docs.src: Source: R. R. Palmer et al., A History of the Modern World, 9th edition, McGraw-Hill
text: . . . The English Revolution of 1688, confirming the ascendancy [rise] of Parliament over the king, meant in economic terms the ascendancy of the more well-to-do property-owning classes. Among these the landowners were by far the most important, though they counted the great London merchants among their allies. For a century and a half, from 1688 to 1832, the British government was substantially in the hands of these landowners—the “squirearchy” or “gentlemen of England.” The result was a thorough transformation of farming, an Agricultural Revolution without which the Industrial Revolution could not have occurred.

Many landowners, seeking to increase their money incomes, began experimenting with improved methods of cultivation and stock raising. They made more use of fertilizers (mainly animal manure); they introduced new implements (such as the drill seeder and horse-hoe); they brought in new crops, such as turnips, and a more scientific system of crop rotation; they attempted to breed larger sheep and fatter cattle.

An improving landlord, to introduce such changes successfully, needed full control over his land. He saw a mere barrier to progress in the old village system of open fields, common lands, and semicollective methods of cultivation. Improvement also required an investment of capital, which was impossible so long as the soil was tilled by numerous poor and custom-bound small farmers. . . .

easier.label: (adapted, easier to read)
text: The English Revolution of 1688 confirmed that Parliament, not the king, held the power. In money terms that meant the richer property-owning classes held it. The most important of these were the landowners, and the great London merchants were their allies. For a century and a half, from 1688 to 1832, the British government was largely in the hands of these landowners — the “squirearchy” or “gentlemen of England.” The result was a complete change in farming, an Agricultural Revolution, without which the Industrial Revolution could not have happened.

Many landowners wanted to earn more money, so they began trying better ways of growing crops and raising animals. They used more fertilizer (mostly animal manure); they brought in new tools (such as the drill seeder and horse-hoe); they brought in new crops, such as turnips, and a more scientific system of crop rotation; they tried to breed larger sheep and fatter cattle.

To make changes like these work, an improving landlord needed full control over his land. He saw a mere barrier to progress in the old village system of open fields, common lands, and shared ways of farming. Improvement also needed money invested, which was impossible while the soil was worked by many poor small farmers bound by custom.

docs.title: Edmund Cartwright and the power loom
docs.src: Source: “Edmund Cartwright & the Invention of the Power Loom,” Our Nottinghamshire, May 9, 2013
text: . . .Once back in Leicestershire, however, Cartwright found that the idea of devising a weaving machine had lodged itself firmly in his mind.

“It struck me,” he wrote, “that as in plain weaving, according to the conception I then had of the business, that as there could only be three movements which were to follow each other in succession, there would be little difficulty in reproducing and repeating them.”
“Full of these ideas I immediately employed a carpenter and smith to carry them into effect. . . . To my great delight, a piece of cloth, such as it was, was the produce. . . .”
Sadly, this first machine of Cartwright's was not at all successful, and was actually slower in its operation than a manual hand loom.
Nevertheless, it worked and proved that producing cotton cloth by mechanical means was a possibility. All Cartwright had to do now was to improve and refine the process.

It took a whole series of improvements and new patents before, finally, in 1788, his machine had reached a point where the three component processes of weaving—shedding, picking and beat-up—could be performed with sufficient speed and efficiency. . . .

easier.label: (adapted, easier to read)
text: … Once back in Leicestershire, though, Cartwright found that the idea of building a weaving machine had lodged itself firmly in his mind.

“It struck me,” he wrote, “that in plain weaving, from what I understood of the business then, there could only be three movements, one after another, so there would be little difficulty in reproducing and repeating them.”
“Full of these ideas I immediately employed a carpenter and smith to carry them out. … To my great delight, a piece of cloth, such as it was, was the result. …”
Sadly, this first machine of Cartwright's was not at all successful, and was actually slower to work than a hand loom worked by a person.
Even so, it worked, and it proved that making cotton cloth by machine was possible. All Cartwright had to do now was improve and refine the process.

It took a whole series of improvements and new patents before, finally, in 1788, his machine reached the point where the three parts of weaving — shedding, picking and beat-up — could be done fast and well enough. …

docs.title: Andrew Ure on steam engines
docs.src: Source: Andrew Ure, The Philosophy of Manufactures: or, an Exposition of the Scientific, Moral, and Commercial Economy of the Factory System of Great Britain, A. M. Kelley
text: . . . Steam-engines furnish the means not only of their support but of their multiplication. They create a vast demand for fuel; and, while they lend their powerful arms to drain the pits and to raise the coals, they call into employment multitudes of miners, engineers, ship-builders, and sailors, and cause the construction of canals and railways: and, while they enable these rich fields of industry to be cultivated to the utmost, they leave thousands of fine arable fields free for the production of food to man, which must have been otherwise allotted to the food of horses. Steam-engines moreover, by the cheapness and steadiness of their action, fabricate [produce] cheap goods, and procure [acquire] in their exchange a liberal supply of the necessaries and comforts of life, produced in foreign lands. . . .

easier.label: (adapted, easier to read)
text: … Steam-engines provide the means not only of their own upkeep but of their multiplication. They create a huge demand for fuel; and while they lend their powerful arms to drain the pits and raise the coal, they put to work crowds of miners, engineers, ship-builders and sailors, and cause canals and railways to be built. While they let these rich fields of industry be worked to the utmost, they leave thousands of good arable fields free to grow food for people, which would otherwise have had to grow food for horses. Steam-engines also, because they work cheaply and steadily, fabricate [produce] cheap goods, and procure [acquire] in exchange for them a generous supply of the necessaries and comforts of life, produced in foreign lands. …

docs.title: The Liverpool and Manchester Railway
docs.src: Sources: Encyclopaedia Britannica and Wikipedia, “Liverpool and Manchester Railway” (adapted)
text: The Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened on September 15, 1830. It ran about 30 miles between the port of Liverpool and the mill town of Manchester. It was the first railway to run scheduled passenger and freight trains pulled only by steam locomotives. Huge loads of raw materials for the textile mills came into Liverpool by ship and went on by rail.
